1.pericope_label: The birth, naming, circumcision and weaning of Isaac

schools.summary: Calvin makes the promise the necessary starting point for reading the birth, hears a deliberate emphasis in the repeated 'as he had spoken', defends Abraham's naming as heraldry rather than invention, turns the circumcision into an argument that men may not multiply sacraments beyond the two Christ left, dismisses the rabbinic tale of infants brought for Sarah to suckle, and rejects Augustine's explanation of why the feast fell at the weaning; Gill supplies the narrative frame.

Henry reads the delay as proof that mercies come at God's time rather than ours, holds that human invention should yield to the plainness of divine institution in the naming, matches God's punctuality in promising with Abraham's in obeying, draws four senses from the name, and makes Sarah's nursing a pattern for women of quality who have nurses at hand.

Clarke takes Sarah's laughter for a joy that suspends the reason, comparing the disciples who believed not for joy, and turns the weaning into an excursion on the etymology of the English word and the disputed age at which children were weaned; Wesley follows Henry closely on the strength given to conceive and on the seal of the covenant.

Ellicott notes that the promise is given by Elohim and the fulfilment credited to Jehovah, marks two departures from later usage in the naming, and reports the surviving eastern custom of feasting at a weaning; Keil and Delitzsch supply the transition, that the object of holy laughter was made the butt of unholy wit.

debates: Why the feast was held at the weaning rather than at the birth or circumcision, and at what age children were weaned
outliers: Calvin rejects both Augustine's explanation of the weaning feast and the rabbinic story about Sarah suckling other infants

9.pericope_label: Ishmael mocks, Sarah demands his expulsion, and Abraham is grieved

schools.summary: Calvin locates the offence in the word, since the participle for Ishmael and the name Isaac share a root and both are sons of laughter in opposite senses, answers Paul's charge of persecution by the scorn of a tongue that pierces the soul, concedes Sarah spoke imperiously while holding her words a divine oracle, and judges that Abraham's affection was trying to confound a distinction God had drawn.

Henry notes the domestic aggravation of a boy fourteen years the elder abusing a child who was no match for him, warns that God observes what children do in play, reads the quarrel as the standing enmity of the two seeds, and takes Sarah's sentence for a prophecy against all who hold a place in the visible church without the new birth.

Clarke reports the Targums' charge of idolatry and other guesses only to dismiss conjecture as useless and endless, and softens Sarah's demand by arguing that the verb means to divorce as well as to expel, so that a legal bar to the inheritance was what she sought.

Ellicott fixes the offence between gross wickedness and harmless play, explains it from Ishmael's fourteen years as heir and blames polygamy for such jealousies, argues that 'bondwoman' unduly depresses Hagar and with her the Jewish church in Paul's allegory, and observes that Abraham thought the demand unjust; Keil and Delitzsch settle the sense of 'in Isaac shall seed be called'.

debates: What Ishmael's mocking amounted to, and whether Sarah's demand was just
outliers: Ellicott judges the Authorised rendering 'bondwoman' misleading, and reads the whole quarrel as a consequence of polygamy rather than of either party's fault

12.pericope_label: God confirms the sentence, and Abraham sends Hagar and Ishmael away

schools.summary: Calvin explains that God endorses Sarah's demand for his own work's sake rather than for her temper, warns that Paul's allegory is no licence for Origen's method of torturing every history into one, reads the two sons as the standing condition of the church and turns the firstborn's vain title against the boast of apostolic succession, measures the cost of the obedience as a tearing out of the bowels, and asks why the provision was so slender; Gill traces Ishmael's nation and refuses the Targum's description of it as a people of thieves.

Henry praises the manner of the obedience above the act, speedy at daybreak after a night's vision and submissive against Abraham's own judgment, and holds that Hagar and Ishmael forfeited a place they had abused.

Clarke vindicates Sarah's counsel and shows by arithmetic that Ishmael was about seventeen, so the appearance of cruelty rests on a misreading; Wesley goes furthest of any in the other direction, denying that the expulsion was Ishmael's ruin and calling it presumption to shut all who fall outside the external covenant out of every mercy.

Ellicott renders the promise as naming the seed that shall be accounted Abraham's, notes that Hagar is never acknowledged as his wife, and shows from usage that the word translated child carries no implication of age.

debates: Whether exclusion from the covenant line implies exclusion from mercy altogether
outliers: Wesley expressly refuses to read Ishmael's expulsion as his eternal ruin, against the severity of Calvin's account of the two seeds

15.pericope_label: Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness, and the well that saved them

schools.summary: Calvin asks why the boy's cry was heard and not the mother's weeping, refuses to assume either was penitent, and answers from the promise made to Abraham; he hears a reproof in the angel's question, takes the well to have been there all along and draws from it that we must ask for prudence to see the help beside us, and reads even Ishmael's marriage as a submission to his mother that shames those who overthrow the rights of nature; Gill reports the rabbinic accounts of the failing water and of the well, and checks a traveller's description of Paran against the fact that Ishmael lived there.

Clarke explains on physiological grounds why a youth failed before his mother, reads the casting down as sheltering him from the heat, and takes the opened eyes to mean only that God directed her to water near at hand; Wesley observes that no word of Ishmael's is recorded, only sighs that cried loud in the ears of mercy.

Ellicott narrates the whole episode closely, explains Ishmael's weakness from the longer lives of that age, follows Abravanel in holding the well already existed, reads the command to hold him by the hand as pointing to her future protection, and notes what Ishmael's choice of the desert implied; Keil and Delitzsch place Paran, refuse to force the verb about his growth, and join Ellicott in marking that the angel here is of Elohim where before it was of Jehovah.

debates: Whether the well was created for Hagar or merely shown to her

22.pericope_label: Abimelech seeks a covenant, and Abraham reproves him about the well

schools.summary: Calvin asks why so moderate a man drew suspicion and answers from heathen anxiety and the size of his household, explains the clipped grammar of the oath, wonders that Abraham had not sought redress earlier while praising his patience under what amounted to an attempt on his life, and reads the sheep and oxen as tribute freely offered, resolving the difficulty of a promised heir acknowledging another lord by the fact that possession had not yet come.

Henry sees the promise of a great name fulfilled in a landless sojourner's friendship being courted, takes the king's testimony as proof that God's favour can be visible to neighbours, and defends Abraham's readiness to swear on the ground that religion should not make men sour to all company.

Clarke reports the Chaldee's rendering as the Word of Jehovah and compares it with the Johannine Logos, describes the rite of passing between the pieces, traces the rule of like for like to Abimelech's appeal, explains the value of wells in that country, and suggests the cattle were sacrifices Abraham gave the king to offer.

Ellicott identifies Abimelech and Phichol as official titles, dates the visit to a cooling of relations over the herdsmen, judges Abraham's earlier conduct toward Sarah the worse by contrast with the king's generosity, glosses the phrase for son and son's son as an idiom for kith and kin, and reconstructs the indirect diplomacy of the interview; Keil and Delitzsch record that the king had not heard of the seizure until that day.

debates: Why Abraham had not complained of the stolen well sooner, and whether the covenant was between equals
outliers: Ellicott reads the episode as showing Abraham's earlier treatment of Sarah in a worse light, where the other sources pass it over

28.pericope_label: The seven ewe lambs, the naming of Beersheba, and the everlasting God

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the king's authority was needed to secure a stranger's well, rejects the theory that the lambs were coins of that shape, defends deriving Beersheba from the oath while allowing the whole covenant is comprised in the name, notices that a man who had shifted his tent for sixty years is never before said to have planted a shrub, and hears in the title of the everlasting God a disclaimer that Abraham's confidence rested on an earthly king; Gill collects the rabbinic guesses about the grove and traces the later abuse of groves to such beginnings.

Henry observes that Abraham knew when he was well off and yet remained a pilgrim, and makes the closing act an open profession which his neighbours could share, since good men should propagate their goodness and not merely keep it.

Clarke reads the lambs as the price and the witness of Abraham's title, turns the word for the tree into an excursion on sacred oaks from Romulus to the Druids with Pliny on the mistletoe, adopts Shuckford's correction that the Hebrew means to invoke in the name rather than to call upon it, and argues that the word for everlasting admits no limited sense without consequences for the blessed as well as the lost.

Ellicott derives the seven lambs from a verb meaning to be sevened, weighs whether Abimelech's question was ignorance or courtesy, reports Robinson's identification of the site and the rope-worn parapets still there, and traces a progression in Abraham's names for God from the supreme to the almighty to the eternal; Keil and Delitzsch identify the tamarisk and make its hard evergreen wood a type of enduring covenant grace.

debates: Whether Beersheba means the well of the oath or the well of seven
outliers: Clarke follows Shuckford in judging the Authorised rendering of the phrase 'called on the name of the LORD' very erroneous
